#2818. Binance breach puts custody at center of crypto infrastructure trade

The $6.3 billion Binance hack could accelerate a shift in how investors value cryptocurrency companies, putting a greater premium on custody providers and the infrastructure needed to securely hold and protect digital assets.

Much of crypto's evolution this year has involved companies moving past their reliance on trading volumes and transaction fees, to focus instead on building the infrastructure connecting digital assets with traditional finance. Last Thursday's breach adds a new dimension, bringing cybersecurity, custody, compliance and balance-sheet resilience into sharper focus.

Importantly, the Binance breach was not an indictment of crypto itself, or a case of leadership-driven fraud, as with FTX in late 2022. Instead, Binance's leadership moved quickly to contain the fallout, protect customers and commit the exchange's own resources to cover losses.

On Tuesday, Binance CEO Richard Teng told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" that the company has replenished 98% of $6.34 billion in affected assets, and that it is still in the process of purchasing outstanding, more illiquid assets.

Management's response, alongside efforts elsewhere in the industry to boost confidence, helped prevent a security breach from escalating into a broader crisis of confidence. For example, Tether, Circle, Ripple and others moved quickly to freeze or restrict access to about $3 billion in stolen assets; Coinbase blocked transfers to compromised wallets and offered Binance direct assistance.

The hack could even help shape the next phase of the crypto infrastructure trade. The new winners may not just be the businesses with the most users, volume or assets under custody, but the ones that can also demonstrate they're able to protect those assets under extreme duress.

"Which company has the resources to invest in cybersecurity and protect customer funds? For a smaller company, it could be much harder because once these crypto companies become infrastructure plays, providing the well for tokenization … they need to have the compliance and control in place so that a similar hacking will not happen or can be minimized," Owen Lau, senior analyst at ClearStreet, told CNBC. "Larger companies have more resources that could give them some advantage."

While institutional investors have increasingly embraced digital assets, broader adoption depends on confidence that those assets can be securely held, accessed and transferred. The Binance breach highlights the importance of that infrastructure, and could increase demand for specialized custodians and platforms with established asset-protection capabilities.

Coinbase has operated a dedicated institutional custody business since 2018. Circle entered the custody business this year, after the U.S. Office of the Comptroller of the Currency granted it approval to operate as a trust bank. In the past few years, Ripple and Kraken have also launched custody businesses.

Still, smaller players compete in the space as well. Small cap crypto exchange stock Gemini Space Station has offered custody services since 2019. BitGo Holdings, founded in 2013, is one of the earliest players in institutional crypto custody and infrastructure, with a reputation for security and serving major institutions.

The shift could also drive consolidation as companies look to buy capabilities, deepen their infrastructure offerings and achieve the scale needed to compete, Lau said.

The more consequential structural shift may be the separation of custody from execution, according to Morgan Stanley.

"Crypto exchanges have historically combined trading, custody, and settlement within vertically integrated platforms, concentrating operational risk. Repeated security breaches could encourage investors to move assets toward independent custody while continuing to trade on CEXs," the firm's analyst Felix Stratmann said in a note Monday," referring to centralized cryptocurrency exchanges.

"This would preserve the role of centralized exchanges as liquidity and execution venues, while potentially benefiting regulated custodians, including banks, as institutional investors place greater emphasis on asset segregation, operational resilience, and investor protection," Stratmann said.

#2815. One move the Rockets must make this season

The Houston Rockets are off to their best start since their franchise record-setting 2017-18 season. That season, of course, featured Chris Paul and the Rockets' second-best player in franchise history, James Harden. The Rockets won a franchise-best 65 games that season, and it was also the last time they made the Western Conference Finals.

The Rockets have gone through a complete overhaul since then and were hoping they could get back to that level or beyond with the hiring of Ime Udoka in 2023. The Rockets have made progress, going from a rebuilding lottery team after Harden was traded to the Brooklyn Nets in 2021 to a playoff team the last two seasons.

Unfortunately for the Rockets, they have plateaued over the last two seasons, bowing out in the first round in both seasons. There were legitimate reasons for that, as the Rockets made the playoffs for the first time in four seasons in 2024, and last season they were without not only Fred VanVleet, who was out all season, but also Kevin Durant, who missed all but one playoff game.

Heading into this season, the Rockets plan to have a full roster for the first time in the Kevin Durant era. VanVleet was ready to start the season, along with Steven Adams, who missed the last four months with a lower-body injury. Those plans lasted one game into the regular season, as Adams went on the injury report with a right soleus (calf) injury. Udoka stated that Adams is not day-to-day but week-to-week.

Clint Capela is the Rockets' third-string center and filled in for Adams last season after he went down in January, and he filled that role again at the start of this season. Capela is now a two-time Rocket who started his career with the team and played during the Harden era; he had some good games filling in for Adams this season, but the 32-year-old is now also out with an ankle injury.

Even after their loss Wednesday night to the shorthanded Minnesota Timberwolves, the Rockets are still 7-2 and are one of the early favorites to go deep into the playoffs. They have their most versatile team since that 2017-18 team and improved their bench this past offseason. However, the backup center position is the one position the Rockets may need to improve before the trade deadline, and with their assets, they are in a great position to do so.

First off, Adams, when healthy, is one of the best, if not the best, backup centers in the NBA. Since he arrived in Houston, he has catapulted them into the league's best rebounding team every season he's been on the roster. When Adams went out with his injury in January of last season, the Rockets' rebounding dropped noticeably for the rest of the season.

The issue is that Adams' availability isn't guaranteed, as he missed several months last season and has played only one game this season. Even before coming to the Rockets, Adams missed the entire 2023-24 season, including the second half with the Rockets after being traded before the deadline.

As mentioned earlier, Capela is a serviceable third center, but he is entering his 14th season and is no longer the lob threat he once was. The Rockets do have another center, Oscar Tshiebwe, who has been good in limited minutes but doesn't offer what the Rockets lack: an athletic lob threat at center.

The Rockets have the most assets in the 2027 draft, as they can swap picks with the Nets and also have the Phoenix Suns' first-round pick. Both teams are off to slow starts this season: the Suns are 1-5, and the Nets are 2-6. One quick note: in past seasons, teams that finished in the bottom three in wins had the best odds at a top pick; that is not the case now, as finishing with the worst record gives you only two ping-pong balls, and finishing 4-10 actually gives you better odds.

The Rockets having those two picks is a big deal, and they may use them as part of a bigger trade, but if they continue their current trajectory, they may feel they dont have to swing for the fences and may go for a smaller move, like upgrading their backup center.

As mentioned earlier, the Rockets need a center who is reliable and, more importantly, can run the floor, block shots, and play above the rim or, at the very least, stretch the court. The best move is to hold onto Adams, since he is still the best backup big when he is on the court, and bringing in another center can help the Rockets slowly bring him back.

Some realistic names to consider, even though each comes with its own drawbacks.

Robert Williams has long been on the trade block. The 6'9 "center is one of the most athletic centers in the league. He would provide the Rockets with a rim-running big who can play above the rim. However, he also suffers from the same injury issues as Adams.

Williams has played only 85 games in the previous three seasons and is the most expensive player on this list at $14 million a year. That would mean you'd likely have to trade Adams, and the best-case scenario would be if you can hold on to him, as he can still have a positive impact, especially in the playoffs.

PHILADELPHIA, PA – NOVEMBER 2: Jalen Smith #25 of the Chicago Bulls shoots the ball during the game against the Philadelphia 76ers on November 2, 2026 at Xfinity Mobile Arena in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and/or using this Photograph, user is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Jesse D. Garrabrant/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images

Jalen Smith, who currently plays for the Chicago Bulls, is more of a stretch big and a good shot blocker. Smith tied his career-high from the 3-point range, shooting .373. The Rockets haven't had a center who can stretch the floor in a long time, and Smith could provide exactly that off the bench. Smith is also only making nine millon a season, which is a more manageable trade contract.

The drawback is that Smith is in the last year of his contract. Which means he could walk after this season, especially if he is looking for a starting role next season, which he wouldn't have in Houston.

NEW YORK, NY – NOVEMBER 2: Day'Ron Sharpe #20 of the Brooklyn Nets shoots the ball during the game against the New York Knicks on November 2, 2026 at Madison Square Garden in New York City, New York. Day'Ron Sharpe is another center who could be on the trade block as the Nets continue to rebuild. Sharpe is the youngest of the three. Sharpe is an offensive rebounding machine who can run the floor and has increased his outside shooting. Sharpe would give the Rockets a young, mobile backup center they haven't had in many years. Sharpe contract is also manageable at only 10 millon a season for the next two seasons.

Sharpe doesn't provide Smith's outside shooting, but he can crash the boards with the best in the NBA and gives you a version of Adams when he is on the court. He's also under contract for two seasons instead of one like Smith.

As mentioned above, the Rockets may hold onto the picks and see what happens next offseason, or use them for a blockbuster move before the deadline. If they do decide to go one of those routes, backup center is still a position they should look to upgrade this season.

#2811. Democratic sweep puts crypto on defensive in Washington

Democrats' sweep of Congress likely resets the political calculus for crypto, ushering in a more adversarial approach in Washington and pushing industry-friendly legislation like the Clarity Act to the back burner.

With crypto critics like Sherrod Brown, D-Ohio, returning to the Senate and Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., retaining significant influence over financial policy, analysts say the new Congress is likely to focus on scrutinizing President Donald Trump's personal crypto dealings over supportive industry legislation.

For years, crypto fought an uphill battle in Washington, asking for clear operating rules, but often landing on the receiving end of regulation by enforcement. That shifted after Trump's 2024 election victory, giving the industry a reprieve and seat at the policy table.

"We see Sherrod Brown winning in Ohio as damaging the crypto industry's political clout as the industry worked to defeat him," Jaret Seiberg, TD Cowen's Washington analyst, said in a note Wednesday. "We did not think Clarity could advance over the next two years. This makes us more confident in our prediction."

The crypto industry spent more than $200 million to sway the midterms, hoping to get leaders elected that could push a comprehensive crypto market structure bill over the finish line after the Clarity Act stalled in the Senate.

Seiberg emphasized that Democrats "will investigate Trump's crypto entanglements including World Liberty Financial" and said "the resulting political environment may make it impossible to advance a version of Clarity that the crypto sector could back."

Mike Townsend, Charles Schwab's managing director of legislative and regulatory affairs, said he expects "Democrats to push next year for a version of the bill that is much tougher on cryptocurrency companies."

The stakes extend beyond market structure legislation via Clarity. Stablecoin innovation; decentralized finance, or DeFi, development; banking access; tokenization; and sensible tax policy are priorities the industry sees as important to ensuring the U.S. remains competitive in the global crypto economy.

The industry will need continued bipartisan engagement to ensure these priorities aren't sidelined by changing political dynamics. And Democrats have historically been less supportive of crypto than Republicans, though that divide has narrowed as more Democrats embrace the industry.

The implications of Democrats' big win aren't all bad. Crypto has reached a level of financial integration that could be difficult to reverse, with its future increasingly centered on establishing crypto as financial infrastructure. Even with the Clarity Act potentially stalled until 2028, key financial regulators can help advance the industry through rule-making.

Coinbase's vice president of U.S. policy, Kara Calvert, points out that the election results point to a historic shift in the makeup of the incoming Congress, with a record number of pro-crypto voices expected to join its ranks.

"With last night's results, the 120th Congress is on track to have more new pro-crypto members than we've ever seen in any freshman class," she said. "Crypto is 100% bipartisan, and that's why the future of finance does not rest on either political party or a single election night. Democrats and Republicans alike know that clear rules protect consumers and keep innovation in the U.S."

As of Thursday morning, 19 candidates characterized as pro crypto by the advocacy nonprofit Stand With Crypto have been elected to the Senate versus eight Senate candidates it characterizes as anti crypto. In the House, 228 pro-crypto candidates have been elected versus 106 the group deems anti crypto.

Several races have not been called, but Fairshake — the super PAC launched in 2023 to support pro-crypto candidates regardless of party — has so far won 29 of the 34 races it spent on, per Reuters, including three of the six House candidates it prioritized by spending a baseline of $1 million on their campaigns.

Dante Disparte, chief strategy officer and head of global policy and operations at Circle, emphasized Circle's bipartisan approach and readiness for new Senate and House leadership, but said it "may take longer to get Clarity tabled again."

That bipartisan support may offer a blueprint for what comes next, but even if crypto legislation stalls, progress can continue, said Joseph Chalom, CEO of ether treasury company Sharplink.

"We expect the Clarity Act to remain on hold through 2028. Even so, there is a clear path forward for stablecoins … and for the tokenization of public equities under the SEC's five-year innovation exemption," he said. "Technological progress is rarely rolled back. Once the benefits of faster settlement, lower costs and markets that never close become clear to investors and institutions, this shift will be very difficult to reverse, regardless of who wins the White House in 2028."

Near-term, investors should expect more volatility as the market tries to figure out how crypto regulation may shift under a Democratic Congress.

The impact of the blue wave "should vary considerably across assets," said James Butterfill, head of research at CoinShares. "We would expect U.S. crypto equities to be more sensitive than bitcoin, particularly businesses reliant on new regulatory permissions. Established, compliant operators could even benefit from greater scrutiny of competitors. So miners who already have data centers set up are likely to remain in high demand by AI hyperscalers."

— CNBC's Talia Kaplan contributed reporting.

#2810. ‘Practice what we preach’: Mavs’ second-half fight comes up one possession short at Spurs

For 24 minutes on Wednesday night, the Dallas Mavericks looked like a team with more questions than answers. For the next 24 minutes, though, they looked like a team that had found a winning formula against the reigning Western Conference champs. Despite rallying back from being down 19 points in the second half to take a late three-point lead, the Mavs ultimately came up short in a 112-111 loss to the San Antonio Spurs on the road.

The second consecutive loss dropped Dallas to 4-4 on the season. It's also the Mavs' second loss to San Antonio in less than two weeks, after the Spurs rolled to a 122-106 win in Dallas on Oct. 24 with Cooper Flagg and Kyrie Irving both sidelined.

This one had a different feel, though. Despite Victor Wembanyama going off for 52 points, 24 rebounds and eight blocks, the Mavs still had an opportunity to win the game at the end, but Irving's last-second shot just wouldn't drop. As encouraging as it was to see the Mavs not give up and fight back to make it a close game, nobody seemed happy to come away with any moral victories on Wednesday night.

"I feel like it's a bad thing," Naji Marshall said when asked what it meant to come back from 19 down. "I feel like we're kind of telling ourselves and showing ourselves personally what we're doing wrong. I feel like we're letting ourselves down. Just practice what we preach. Go out there from the jump and play like [how we did in the second half]. Who knows how the game will turn out?"

Irving also spoke about the Mavs' uninspiring first half. San Antonio put up 32 points in the first quarter and 36 more in the second, and Dallas spent most of that stretch, in his words, "playing on our heels."

"We just got back to the identity that we're trying to build for ourselves, which is, you know, it's not so much desperation basketball, but it's just playing to be the hunters," Irving said. "… They were getting a lot of offensive rebounds, a lot of second chances. … The second half, I feel like we hit them and they had to respond, and that's what got us back in the game."

Instead of driving into Wembanyama at the rim, the Mavericks made a big adjustment and started kicking the ball out, re-spacing and letting it fly. Dallas ended up shooting 14-of-37 (37.8 percent) from deep.

"We stopped challenging Wemby at the rim, and started making better decisions with the basketball," Mavs head coach Dusty May said.

This isn't the first time the Mavericks have had to dig out of an early hole this season, and they know that's a problem that needs to be addressed if they want to potentially be a playoff contender this year.

"To start off the game and, you know, give two quarters up, 32 and 36, that's not where we want to be," Irving said. "And when you're giving up that amount of points in the first half, teams are going to be very comfortable and you got to work your way back. … I think we have to start trending in a direction where we're going into halftime with a lead."

#2808. Deion Sanders, Kenny Dillingham ‘better hire’ debate has clear answer before Saturday’s game

The Arizona State Sun Devils and Colorado Buffaloes hired their head coaches about a week apart in late 2022, and the two programs have been measured against each other ever since. With the teams set to meet in Tempe on Saturday, a post from PHNX Sun Devils brought the old argument back this week.

"Do you remember when people were saying Coach Prime was a better hire than Kenny Dillingham? Those people are really quiet these days," PHNX wrote on X.

In December 2022, Fox Sports' Bryan Fischer gave Colorado's hire of Deion Sanders an A grade and Arizona State's hire of Dillingham a B, flagging Dillingham's inexperience as a 32-year-old first-time head coach who had called plays for one season. Ten months later, Colorado was a national TV attraction and Arizona State was sitting on a 1-4 start.

Dillingham is 26-21 at Arizona State after going 3-9, 11-3, 8-5 and 4-4 so far this year. Sanders is 19-26 at Colorado after going 4-8, 9-4, 3-9 and 3-5. Since both programs joined the Big 12 in 2024, Dillingham is 15-8 in league games and Sanders is 9-14.

The 2024 season holds the biggest gap. Arizona State went 11-3 and won its first conference title since 2007 on the way to the College Football Playoff, while Colorado's best year under Sanders ended at 9-4. Sanders still has the bigger contract, with a five-year deal worth a reported $54 million against the five-year extension paying Dillingham $7.5 million a year.

ASU Sun Devils head coach Kenny Dillingham yells out to his team as they play against the Houston Cougars at Mountain America Stadium in Tempe on Oct. 25, 2025.

Those results back the post comfortably, though Colorado did get something else from the hire that the early grades were pricing in, which was attention. Dillingham made that case himself before the teams met last November, when Arizona State won 42-17 in Boulder.

"People are talking about Colorado, recruits want to go to Colorado. They've won, like I said, a high percentage of games with him than before him. He's battled a bunch, and it just shows the type of person he is. He's a fighter and a winner, and that's shown up at Colorado since he's been there," Dillingham said, according to On SI's Jack Carlough.

Arizona State's own season keeps this from being a clean victory lap. The Sun Devils are 4-4 and 2-3 in the Big 12, with losses by 28 to the Texas A&M Aggies, 36 to the Baylor Bears and 28 to the Texas Tech Red Raiders, and they need two wins in their last four games to reach a bowl. Freshman Jake Fette is making his second career start on Saturday after Arizona State moved on from Cutter Boley.

Jul 7, 2026; Frisco, TX, USA; Colorado head coach Deion Sanders speaks to reporters during Big 12 Conference Football Media Days at The Star. Mandatory Credit: Raymond Carlin III-Imagn Images

Some of the doubt has moved to Tempe, and the coach pushing back on it this week was Sanders.

"Coach Dillingham, you all know he's my guy. Came in the same class, (he was) coach of the year in 2024. I read some stuff and I see some stuff every once in a while that they're questioning his ability. Like, did he forget to coach since '24? He's a phenomenal mind. We almost had an opportunity to work together once upon a time, but I'm glad God played it out like he did," Sanders said, according to On SI's Dan Allison.

Colorado comes in at 3-5 after a 27-24 overtime win over the Kansas State Wildcats ended a five-game losing streak. The two coaches are 1-1 against each other, with Colorado's 27-24 win in Tempe in 2023 and last year's game in Boulder, and the third meeting kicks off at 7:30 p.m. ET on ESPN2.

#2807. CNBC's experts on whether the AI trade is ending and what investors should do next

Amid a powerful rout in tech stocks, investors told CNBC on Thursday that something may be fundamentally breaking in the AI trade following the big success of Democrats in Tuesday's midterm elections and the threat they try to slow the data center buildout.

Democrats are more aggressively anti-data center than Republicans, and Wall Street is quickly redoing its math what any restrictions they implement could mean for the related companies' future growth.

"Right now, investors are questioning that $1.2 trillion of capex that we forecast for next year," Peter Boockvar, chief investment officer at One Point BFG Wealth Partners, told CNBC. "Well, maybe that's not going to happen."

Boockvar believes this could be the start of the end of the AI trade as we know it.

Whether it's completely over or not, investors need to be reassessing how they're planning to play the AI trade going forward, the analysts said.

The Nasdaq Composite dropped 5% on Thursday and fell into correction territory, off by more than 11% from its record high set last month. The iShares Semiconductor ETF dropped 11% on Thursday, its biggest decline since during the Covid breakout in March 2020. The Global X Artificial Intelligence & Technology ETF (AIQ) is down 6% on the day and down 15% over the past month.

"There has been a huge change in the outlook for AI infrastructure buildout," Eric Johnston, head of equities at Cantor Fitzgerald, told CNBC. "The entire economy and the consumer and earnings growth are all levered to that buildout."

The selling Thursday spilled over to non-AI stocks with the Dow Jones Industrial average down more than 1,600 points.

Josh Brown pointed to the 4.8% yield for the 10-year Treasury yield, saying a compelling risk-free rate is causing investors to reconsider taking the risk in these volatile AI stocks.

"You don't need to be at 80% U.S. stocks and have 60% of that exposure be tech," Brown said.

Many investors believe the AI trade isn't over completely, investors just need to get more selective.

"The AI buildout just got harder," said Rob Sechan, Newedge Capital Group Founder & Managing Partner:

"Nobody voted to make compute less scarce," Sechan said, citing Microsoft's Azure cloud business growing 48% year over year in its most recent third quarter. That level of growth suggests its capacity constrained, not demand constrained, he said.

"When new capacity gets harder to build, existing capacity becomes more valuable," Sechan said.

Richard Clode, portfolio manager at Janus Henderson, noted a few bright spots in tech on Thursday despite the highly correlated downward movements in the big tech indices.

"Motorola Solutions had some good results," he said. "We're seeing a little bit of rotation into some of the … internet names...Sony reported some good results, and again they were up strongly overnight."

"So there are some brief pockets of respite from this, but obviously pretty painful across the board today," he said.

Some experts believe the selling was overdone and investors could start nibbling.

This "indiscriminate selling" is a "buying opportunity," said Larry Adam, Raymond James chief investment officer. If investors "take a longer term perspective, which is what we do, I think the valuations at today's levels will tend to prove to be a good buying opportunity," he said, urging investors to look at the fundamentals.

Victoria Greene, chief investment officer of G Squared Private Wealth, said she saw some strong supports around the S&P 500's 200-day moving average and was on the lookout for a market bounce following Thursday's rout.

"Typically, the average return is plus about 180 basis points the next day," she said. "The question we have to ask ourselves: Is this a pullback in an uptrend, which is what I believe? Or is this the end-all, be-all [and] the wheels are coming off and everybody just needs to buy T-bills? I don't think we're there yet."

#2804. Angels’ Nightmare Albert Pujols Scenario Is Coming True With GM Search In Limbo

The Los Angeles Angels are in a very weird spot right now. They let go of their manager Kurt Suzuki and their interim general manager John Mozeliak said that he will not be staying on beyond December. The team has not been officially sold to new principal owner Stan Kroenke yet and while it was assumed that would happen at the GM meetings, that is now unclear based on reporting from Jeff Fletcher. The Angels aren't going to hire a new GM until the sale officially goes through and they probably won't hire a new manager until they have a GM in place which means that they are essentially in limbo.

As if things could not get any worse, Albert Pujols is going to interview with the Houston Astros for their managerial vacancy. Pujols has been seen as a logical fit as the manager of the Angels given the fact that he played for the Halos for years and is still technically on their payroll, so if he were to instead end up as the manager of an American League West rival that would really be a gut punch to Los Angeles.

The tough thing is that the Angels can't really do anything about it. They could bring Pujols in to interview, as he did last year, but if they offered him the job without a GM in place that runs the risk that whoever they hire might not get along with Pujols and the two may butt heads. It is standard practice for the GM or president of baseball operations to select the manager so until they hire that person they are basically just frozen.

Pujols has made his desire to manage in the big leagues quite clear. He has managed a Dominican Winter League team and managed the Dominican Republic team during the 2026 World Baseball Classic so he has some coaching experience in addition to his Hall of Fame career as a player. He would make so much sense for an Angels organization that is in desperate need of excitement and could really capitalize on Arte Moreno's departure as majority owner of the franchise.

The product on the field has not been very good for a long time as the Angels have not had a winning season since 2015 and they lost 100 games for the first time in franchise history in 2026. A big name like Pujols could be the guy they need to get things turned around but if he ends up going to the Astros while the Halos are essentially stuck in neutral then he could end up tormenting the franchise for years to come.

#2803. Has Danny Wolf’s breakout game unlocked frontcourt potential?

The Nets cried Wolf. This time, he was telling the truth.

Despite selecting a historic slew of first-round picks in 2025, the Nets had seen just two of those rookies, Egor Demin and Nolan Traore, crack Jordi Fernández's rotation through the first seven games.

Injuries mounted alongside Brooklyn's losses. Entering Wednesday night with a 1-6 record and coming off a deflating loss to the rival Knicks across the river, they were still winless on their home floor. Urgency kicked in.

Noah Clowney suffered a knee injury in the first half and was ruled out for the remainder of the night, joining Demin, Joshua Jefferson, Ben Saraf, and Drake Powell on the inactive list — five rookie-contract players forced to watch from the sidelines (or Long Island).

Before Wednesday, the former 27th pick had logged minutes in just two games. His 27 minutes on the court was less than two-way's Grant Nelson's 35.

But by the second half, he anchored a unit that turned a tight game into an uncontested 114–104 victory, finishing with 13 points, five rebounds, and three assists on 4-of-6 shooting — including two 3-pointers and a game-high +17 in just under 19 minutes.

"Obviously in the NBA, there's going to be times especially early in your career that you might not be in the rotation, and that was the case for me starting the year," Wolf admitted postgame. "Everyone emphasizes and preaches 'you got to be ready' and you hear it over and over… When coach called my name in the second half, I was ready."

It's a small sample size, but when Wolf knocks down shots and makes plays as a secondary facilitator, he gives Brooklyn a distinct way to generate offense in transition. That dynamic starts on the glass: the more defensive stops the Nets string together, the more opportunities Wolf has to snag a rebound and push the pace before opposing defenses can set up.

General manager Sean Marks has long shown an appreciation for frontcourt players who can rebound and push — from Trevor Booker to Ben Simmons to Julius Randle. Wolf fits that modern "grab-and-go" archetype, but adds a legit 3-point stroke to the equation.

"The biggest staple of our team, especially our offensive identity, is supposed to be playing fast," Wolf explained postgame. "We use the terminology 'pace and space' and I feel like there's times with my play style that I can really help us push the ball up the floor, make simple passes, start the break. Momentum is what helps win you a basketball game."

The sequence that swung Wednesday night's game highlighted that approach. Moments after checking in during the third quarter, Wolf snagged a defensive rebound, pushed the pace, and initiated a transition drive that resulted in a Julius Randle AND-1 layup. On the next possession, he trailed the play, spotted up behind the arc, and hit a 24-foot triple to give Brooklyn its first lead of the second half at 61–59, forcing a Charlotte timeout.

To make it work, Fernández sat three-time All-Star Julius Randle down the stretch in favor of the rookie. Crucially, Fernández didn't deploy Wolf as a standalone center.

Wolf played every single minute alongside a traditional interior anchor — logging 15 minutes and 37 seconds next to Day'Ron Sharpe and 2 minutes and 59 seconds alongside Moritz Wagner.

Protecting Wolf from heavy low-post drop coverage and rim-protection duties allowed him to roam freely and make decisions in the open floor. During Wolf's 15:37 alongside Sharpe, the Nets outscored Charlotte 46-32 (+14), with Wolf racking up 10 of his 13 points, all five of his rebounds, and two of his three assists.

The framework for utilizing a player with Wolf's skillset is familiar to Fernández from his time under Michael Malone in Denver.

"I think that you have to be creative with players that are uncommon," Fernández said in Oct. 2025. "I was very fortunate to work with Nikola [Jokic], and we had to let him show us what he was able to do. Otherwise, if you see him as a traditional player, then you could fail… Nikola showed certain things that were so different for his position and a seven-footer, and that's why he makes all these plays and plays in situations where no other big man plays."

It isn't about becoming the next Jokic, though. Wolf finding his footing in the NBA has required him adjusting from his heavy-usage roles at Yale and Michigan, where his playmaking came from high volume.

"I think that the coaches [at Michigan] didn't even know what my role was going to be," Wolf also said in Oct. 2025. "At Yale, I was more of a traditional 5, and then at Michigan, I don't even know what you would call my position or how I played… In the NBA, it's about continuing to get better within the confines of the roles your coach wants you to play."

On Wednesday, that work in progress delivered real results.

Wolf opened the fourth quarter by hitting a 25-foot transition jumper off a pass from Terance Mann. Operating out of the high-post, he delivered a crisp pass to Traore for a driving floater before driving into the lane himself for an And-1 layup. When Charlotte made a late push, Wolf secured a key offensive rebound, drew the foul, and sank both free throws to seal the victory.

Michael Porter Jr. echoed that praise in the locker room.

"I ain't gonna lie, the difference tonight was Terance Mann and Danny Wolf. They haven't been in rotation much, they came in ready to play… Danny coming in and contributing right away like that, that takes a lot of readiness and a lot of discipline to not play for so many games, come in the second half, and contribute the way he did. I always thought Danny was a special player, and I've said that since he got here."

During his first Summer League in August 2025, Wolf said he's a "work in progress." Now, some of the progress is tangible and helping lead to wins.

#2798. Did Miami finally start to find its defensive identity?

INGLEWOOD, Calif. — "The guys earned their ice. We haven't really earned our ice many times."

That's how Heat coach Erik Spoelstra described his team's effort in a 117-116 win over the Clippers Wednesday night. As the Heat stumbled out of the gate to a 2-5 start this season, the headlines focused on Giannis Antetokounmpo and Bam Adebayo playing next to each other more than off each other, and on how the offense looked clunky. Spoelstra knew that wasn't the issue, it was the bottom-five defense in the league that was keeping the Heat from finding its identity and winning games.

"You have to make plays defensively, and that's what we've been trying to do is find our identity," Spoelstra said. "The offensive stuff like that's way overblown. You know, going into this game, we have almost a top 10 ranked offense [11th in net rating]. That's ahead of where I thought it would be at this time. But our defense is way behind. That's why we lost games."

For 29 minutes Wednesday night in Los Angeles, from the start of the third quarter through Klay Thompson's overtime game-winner, the Miami Heat found that identity.

Miami used its length and athleticism to pressure the Clippers' ballhandlers up the court, switched pick-and-rolls more — and more effectively — than they have all season, and played bully ball against a team light on shot creation. Davion Mitchell was ripping the ball away from Darius Garland.

They looked like the team Spoelstra envisioned — a team that played intense, high-energy defense and would get enough offense from its stars. A team with a defense-first, gritty identity and turned that defense into offense.

"I think we turned it up in the second half, majorly," Thompson said. "That ball pressure at half court that Bam, Giannis, Davion, Pella [Larsson], Ryan [Conwell] had was just a game changer."

"One game, does that solve everything? No, but at least now we can see," Spoelstra said. "All right, this is what the plan was the first day of training camp. Everybody wrapped their mind around it, and it just hasn't gone according to plan. But you could see the efforts. The guys earned their ice."

They earned that ice in the second half — the second quarter was more of what had the Heat losing games to start the season. The Clippers went on a 30-4 run to open the frame and dropped a 43-point second quarter on the Heat, with Garland carving them up as LA shot 16-of-22 in the quarter, including hitting 6-of-7 in the paint and 8-of-13 from 3. The Clippers had a 172 offensive rating in the second quarter as they got the shots they wanted — 75% of their first half shots came at the rim or from 3 (and they were hitting those deep balls).

"We gave up 67 points in the first half, and we just really wanted to try to prove to ourselves that we could do something tough," Spoelstra said. "And we opened up the third quarter, had a really good defensive quarter, held them to 20 points, and then did it again, held them to 20 points in the fourth before overtime."

Miami did it for a night, but now comes the hard part: Doing it again. Especially on Thursday night, going up to the Bay Area for a back-to-back against a Warriors team finding their identity and with a pretty good shooter of their own in the backcourt.

"That's our identity. That's what we have to be. Not every other night. We gotta be there every night," Adabayo said of the second-half defensive effort. "We're not scoring, we gotta make sure they don't score either... Being disruptive, we were flying around. That's what it takes... It's gonna be moments when it's uncomfortable. So being able to get out of that comfort zone and then communicate, you see what the potential is."

Miami now has to live up to that defensive potential nightly — but the second half against the Clippers showed them the path.

Shedeur Sanders is getting closer to being named the starter for Week 9 against the Saints.

#2793. JJ McCarthy Swipes at O’Connell After Vikings Shelve Kyler Murray

Quarterback JJ McCarthy of the New York Giants. Getty

CBS Sports's Garrett Podell named the Minnesota Vikings a potential landing spot for Dallas Cowboys wide receiver George Pickens. Getty

The Minnesota Vikings are moving Kyler Murray to the bench this week against the Buffalo Bills, while JJ McCarthy prepares to start his second contest for the New York Giants in Philadelphia — and the mud on this particular set of circumstances happens to be thick.

Major questions exist as to whether minor hamstring tightness — which did not require Murray to leave the game against the Detroit Lions last week — is the real reason for Carson Wentz's promotion to QB1 in Minnesota this week, or if it's because Murray has struggled mightily and the likes of Justin Jefferson and Jordan Addison are starting to display their frustrations publicly.

And while Minnesota and Murray are attempting to navigate their first loss of the season, McCarthy has suddenly found himself the starter on an NFC division leader and coming off a 20-of-28 performance for 252 yards and zero turnovers against a talented Houston Texans defense.

Never one who appeared to lack for confidence, McCarthy met with media members in New York on Wednesday, November 4 ahead of a showdown with the Eagles (2-6) and spoke glowingly of Giants offensive coordinator Matt Nagy and his system.

Some have taken those comments as a backhanded slight against Vikings head coach and play-caller Kevin O'Connell, who backed off what had been ardent support for McCarthy in 2025 before the team's new general manager, Nolan Teasley, traded the 23-year-old QB for a paltry fifth-round pick in late September.

GettyQuarterback JJ McCarthy of the New York Giants.

McCarthy, now 1-0 as a starter in New York and coming off five strong quarters plus a bye week to rest and prepare for a banged-up Philly squad, had the following to say to reporters on Thursday.

"I absolutely love his play calling and how he adapts with the flow of the game," McCarthy said of Nagy. "Like, he has a beautiful idea and vision going into the game, and most of the time it carries out."

"There's times where he's got to pivot, and seeing him pivot in the last month that I've been here, it's been really exciting to see and just an honor to play for him and go execute the football plays with the ten guys with me in that huddle," McCarthy added. "Gonna continue to do that."

GettyMinnesota Vikings head coach Kevin O'Connell.

Meanwhile, multiple members of the Vikings' coaching staff spoke with Dan Graziano of ESPN last week in Detroit about McCarthy's new opportunity in New York and the potential fallout if he continues to play well and Murray keeps on struggling.

"Minnesota coaches told me they believed McCarthy had matured significantly since the start of the 2026 offseason … and they were happy the team had been able to send him to a place where he had a chance to be successful," Graziano wrote.

"They also recognize they have a chance to look bad if McCarthy plays well for the Giants and Kyler Murray doesn't get things going in Minnesota, but everyone agrees it was time for a scenery change," Graziano continued.

#2791. Raiders special teams’ resounding response key in Week 8 road victory

One of the mountainous tasks on Joe DeCamillis' when he became the chosen special teams boss for Klint Kubiak's Las Vegas Raiders: Increased electricity in the return game.

We saw quite the lightning bolt from DeCamillis' Silver & Black special teams unit this past Sunday in Week 8 against the host New York Jets.

Trailing 13-7 early in the second quarter after Jets quarterback Geno Smith connected with slot receiver Isaiah Williams on an 18-yard touchdown (Raiders rookie cornerback Jermod McCoy was burnt on the play and even held to no avail), Dylan Laube made his presence known — emphatically — taking the ensuing kickoff 95 yards to the house.

The reserve running back and top-flight return man became the first Raider to return a kickoff for a touchdown since fleet-footed wide receiver Jacoby Ford last did it 2011. But that's not all. The 27-year-old sixth-round pick from the 2024 NFL Draft became the first return man in the NFL to house a kickoff this season.

While the 14-13 advantage for Las Vegas turned out to be momentary — New York scored a touchdown on the following possession to take a 20-14 lead) — the special teams score was a much-needed defibrillator for the flatlined Raiders. And the big play came from a Raider that was perceived as a back-end-at-best or cut-day causality in Laube.

But I've long noted that the 5-foot-9 and 204-pound New Hampshire product is a versatile special teamer, as did DeCamillis all offseason and training camp as the Silver & Black prepped for the 2026 campaign.

"Yeah, so, I think once again, my role is to kind of bring that juice every single time and I try to make it with a tackle, with a return, with a block," Laube said when asked about his special teams prowess despite being a running back by trade. "So I try to do everything I can to make something happen because any big play on special teams just kind of fires up the crowd, the offense, the defense too. So it's a special kind of play."

Laube turning on the afterburners above is without question an electrifying play. The kick return unit as a whole came together, particularly reserve safety Isaiah Pola-Mao (No. 20) and reserve tight end Ian Thomas (80). Take a look at the lane Laube took advantage off down the sideline. That was opened up with a combo seal block by Pola-Mao and Thomas to spring the Raiders' return man.

It showcases that it does require a team effort to attain victory and as quarterback Kirk Cousins noted during the postgame press conference, that's something Las Vegas needs more of to stack wins.

"It's complementary football. Especially when you go on the road, to be able to have that seven-point gift given to your offense and get the wind at your back makes a big difference," the veteran signal caller said of Laube's touchdown. "It's what winning football teams do. There are so many different ways to win in this league. I was really happy for Dylan, like you mentioned, coming back to where he grew up. He had so many people here as well, like Mike, and that had to be a special moment for his family, too."

The Jets ended up kicking to Laube three times last Sunday and the halfback produced a total of 144 yards for an impressive 48 yards per return average. In terms of league-wide stature, the 208th pick of the 2024 draft boasts the top 34.1 yards per return average in the NFL (15 returns for 579 yards, long of 95).

Buffalo Bills running back Ray Davis is second with a 31.0 average (10 returns for 310 yards, long of 70) followed by San Francisco 49ers tailback Jordan James 30.0 average (10 returns for 300 yards, long of 39).

For reference, Tennessee Titans wider receiver Chimere Dike leads the league in kick returns with 32 for 829 (25.9 average, with a long of 40).

Laube also nearly blocked a Jets field goal attempt and had an impact tackle during a kick return by New York where he strongly dropped Williams after the Raiders took a 35-30 lead. It was a strong special teams performance overall.

"He's back home, you know, a lot of family here, so it was cool for him to have that moment. Dylan is a stud player for us," Kubiak said after the Jets game. "He continues to make plays, and as you continue to make plays the expectations continue to rise and he's earned that."

Another special teamer that had a resounding response in the much-needed road victory: Place kicker Matt Gay.

Holding a precarious 35-33 lead with 31 seconds left to play, the CBS broadcast openly talked about punting the ball deep to pin the Jets deep. The cameras caught Kubiak watching the clock tick down before calling timeout and having a word with DeCamillis on the sideline. And yes, Las Vegas did send punter AJ Cole III onto the field, but in his other role as holder for Gay's 53-yard field goal attempt. And the veteran drilled it down the middle with room to spare.

Kubiak was asked the why of this decision when analytics favored punting the ball instead of attempting the field goal.

"I just see him kick in practice. I've seen the clutch kicks that he's made. We were at the line that we had confidence in on that yard line, and we've got to get the ball closer for him offensively. But we had confidence in that," Kubiak noted.

This harkens back on another steep task for DeCamillis: Getting the field goal kicking game back on track.

The 32-year-old Gay was the chosen one by DeCamillis to replace longtime Raiders kicker Daniel Carlson (31 years old) and initially, that was met with skepticism (myself included). Gay was on a downward trend since a strong three-year run with the Los Angeles Rams (2020-22) and was viewed as a scrap-heap type signing by Las Vegas when the team decided not to re-sign Carlson.

That decision, however, has proved fruitful as the Gay-DeCamillis reunion is bringing back the kicker's A-Game, which he had with the Rams because the Raiders current special teams boss was the special teams coordinator during the 2021-22 seasons in Los Angeles.

Gay is 18 of 20 on the year for a (90 percent conversion rate) with a long of 59 yards and is 19-for-19 on extra points. He leads the Raiders in scoring with 73 total points while Carlson was released by the New Orleans Saints this past Tuesday. Carlson had his bouts with inaccuracy in the late stages of his Raider career and was just 8 of 12 (66.7 percent) with the Saints in seven games. He was also 16-for-18 on extra points.

Continued strong performances from DeCamillis' special teams group is required for Las Vegas. Especially as the team heads into a tough four-game stretch that begins with the 49ers this coming Sunday in Santa Clara. Then comes a home game against the Seattle Seahawks and back-to-back road trips to face the Denver Broncos and Cleveland Browns before a Week 13 bye week.

#2790. The Lakers are ‘surfing the wave’ of Luka Dončić’s crazy scoring run right now

It's like déjà vu all over again: Luka Dončić scored at least 40 points and the Los Angeles Lakers rode a vibrant offensive attack to victory.

For the fifth time in six games, Dončić eclipsed the 40-point barrier during Los Angeles' 116-103 win over the Sacramento Kings Wednesday night. The one "hiccup" amid this stretch was a 37-point outing against the Golden State Warriors on Friday. Over that span, the Slovenian is averaging 42.8 points, 8.5 rebounds, 8.3 assists and 1.8 steals while shooting 63.3% on 2-pointers, 44.9% beyond the arc (14.8 attempts per game!) and 89.7% at the charity stripe.

He'll rainbow home deep stepback triples, massage his way into crafty, feathery touch shots, draw tons of fouls and still prime teammates for easy shots with one-of-a-kind passing. Every Lakers game is a spectacle hosted by Dončić — and the supporting cast knows it.

"You can call it a wave, you can call it a tsunami, you can call it whatever you want," Walker Kessler told reporters on Wednesday following the Lakers' third straight win. "He's scoring the ball. If you want to call it a wave, we're surfing the wave a little bit when he's making those shots. I mean he's incredible."

With 308 points through eight games, Dončić became the first player since Michael Jordan (303 points) in 1988 to tally 300-plus in the first eight games of the season, according to NBA Stats. He also recorded his sixth straight game with at least 35 points, five rebounds and five assists to pass Damian Lillard for the longest such streak in league history.

Each night, he seizes control of the action like few others can. In fact, nobody else around the Association can do it like him right now. He is otherworldly dominant and continues etching his name into more rarified company.

"You felt it like in that second quarter," head coach JJ Redick said postgame Wednesday. "I thought, again, we were generating good looks and then he comes down and he makes like three shots in a row that there's five guys in the NBA can make and all of a sudden the tie ball game is a nine-, 10-point lead. The team feeds off that, too, when he has it going like that."

#2789. Joe Brady on cutting S C.J. Gardner-Johnson: "It was the best interests of the football team"

On the day the NFL suspended former Bills safety C.J. Gardner-Johnson for spitting on an opponent, Buffalo coach Joe Brady said the team would not be cutting Gardner-Johnson. After the game that Gardner-Johnson missed, the Bills cut him.

Meeting with reporters on Thursday, Brady explained the reversal.

“There was a lot to evaluate,” Brady said. “You know, we got together and figured out, ‘Hey, this is what we felt like this was the best thing to do for the Buffalo Bills.’ I have so much love for [C.J.]. Like, I really do. I loved getting to coach him. I loved being around him. I loved — I did love the edge, and his personality allowing him to be him, right?, and as a person. So that didn’t make the decision easy at all.

“But we also have to be an organization that, you know, it’s unfortunate obviously what happened, you know? But it also opened a door and an opportunity for guys the other day, and that was a part of evaluation. And seeing how those guys kind of played, and you know with a lot of the roster moves. And, again, this wasn’t — we didn’t come out of the game post Vegas and say, ‘This is what we were going to do. We’re just gonna do this the following Monday.’ We were, you know, the plan was him being here and we were going to evaluate it after the game in Baltimore. And we felt like with some of the moving parts we had to do it was the best interests of the football team.”

Gardner-Johnson’s suspension opened the door for Damar Hamlin to start the game against the Ravens. And Hamlin apparently did well enough to help the Bills realize that, all things considered, the “best interests” of the Bills meant the Bills were better off without the “high maintenance” Gardner-Johnson.

#2787. Steelers Insider Shares Verdict on Potential WR Trade

The Pittsburgh Steelers are in an ideal spot at the moment. The team is 6-2 and in the midst of a bye week, sitting in first place in the AFC North.

The bye means the team won't play another game before the November 10 trade deadline. This gives fans plenty of time to come up with potential trades to pitch and discuss.

One area of particular focus is at the wide receiver position. DK Metcalf has been a massive disappointment this season, though he does still lead the team with 378 receiving yards. Yet the next closest actual wide receiver to him on the leaderboard is Germie Bernard with 284 yards.

Aaron Rodgers has relied upon Jaylen Warren, Darnell Washington, and Pat Freiermuth to help pick up the slack. However, the 6-2 start could mean the Steelers want to make a splash and pair Rodgers with a top talent in his final NFL season.

One longtime Steelers insider shut down any optimism of such an addition.

Gerry Dulac covers the Steelers for the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette and recently took on a series of questions during the bye week.

He was directly asked about the chances of the Steelers trading for a receiver in exchange for draft capital. His response?

"They are not doing that," he wrote. "They already did that when they traded for Pittman."

Dulac is of course referring to Michael Pittman Jr., who has only appeared in three games thus far for the Steelers. He has seven receptions for 89 yards and is currently out on injured reserve.

The Steelers traded for Pittman back in March and expected him to be a top contributor alongside Metcalf. That can still happen once he returns, but the early returns are not promising.

The Steelers could always find the perfect deal and prove Dulac wrong. However, the longtime reporter's statement does seem to indicate the 6-2 Steelers have faith that players like Metcalf, Pittman, and even Roman Wilson will step up during the second half of the season.

Both Pittman and Wilson are on IR, so their individual returns can be viewed as a type of late-season acquisition.

Bernard has shown flashes as of late and it appears the true strength of this offense lies with Warren and the running game.

Steelers fans are understandably impatient given the team hasn't won a playoff game since the 2016 season. The front office may simply decide the impending return of someone like Pittman is a better option than a trade at this point in time.

LeBron James of the Philadelphia 76ers looks on during the second half against the Detroit Pistons at Little Caesars Arena in Detroit, Michigan, Nov. 4, 2026. Getty Images

#2780. Brilliant Baur, Deadly Duran and Outstanding Osmand

A well earned win under the Paradise lights as Celtic overcome adversity to deservedly beat Besiktas…

Celtic finally got off the mark in their Europa League campaign by defeating Turkish high-flyers Besiktas 3-2 in an entertaining match under at Paradise.

Martin O'Neill surprised a few folk by naming James Forrest in a three man attack alongside Kasper Hogh and Sebastian Tounekti, as well as handing Jordan Lotomba a rare start at right back at the expense of Colby Donovan, and it seemed to most that he'd given up all hope of advancing on the European stage.

To be fair to the players they stuck to the task and showed some grit and determination, something they've been lacking in a while, but it looked like the same old story when the Turkish side opened the scoring from the penalty rebound ten minutes into the second period after Lotomba mistimed a challenge just inside the box.

Sam Johnstone saved Olaitan's effort but the Besiktas front man tucked home the rebound to silence the home crowd, and suddenly we all feared the worst.

But credit to the Celtic players who reacted positively after going a goal behind, as they frantically went in search of an equaliser which duly arrived courtesy of substitute Callum Osmand who scored with his first touch just 43 seconds after being brought on to give the Bhoys a well deserved equaliser, and now it was well and truly game on.

The introduction of Osmand and Camilo Duran rejuvenated the hoops in an attacking sense, and it was the Colombian who fired Celtic in front with just twelve minutes remaining with a unlikely victory now looking like a realistic prospect.

It's never plain sailing with Celtic though, and the Turkish side equalised on the 85th minute thanks to a superb outside of the box effort from Kokcu, and Celtic Park was silenced once again, apart from the visiting supporters who celebrated wildly. Celtic soon burst that Turkish delight turning it into despair.

The atmosphere changed once again just two minutes later when that man Duran struck from close range with what proved to be the winner, and sent the Celtic support home with a much needed smile on their faces.

There's still much needed work to be done if we want to advance from the group stage, but this was a win of vital importance, and one that will give us some much needed confidence after some woeful performances of late.

How good was Mika Baur? Outstanding and a worthy choice as Man of the Match.

#2776. Development was the plan. So why is Maluach watching from the bench?

After yet another double-digit loss on Wednesday night, this time to the Portland Trail Blazers (again), the Phoenix Suns find themselves at 1-5. They are a team desperately searching for an identity. Players are trying to establish defined roles, while the coaching staff continues experimenting with combinations in hopes of finding something that can ultimately translate into success.

When you take a step back and look at the bigger picture as it pertains to the Suns' future, things begin to look rather grim. Between the significant amount of dead cap money on the books and the fact that Phoenix has surrendered control of its draft assets for the next several seasons, there was one thing we understood entering this year that could help keep the franchise competitive: development.

After all, continuity and development were the two pillars this organization leaned on throughout the summer. The belief was that returning so many familiar faces would provide a foundation for improvement, while the younger players would take meaningful steps forward in their progression. That was the formula. That was the plan. Yet through six games, the continuity has been noticeably absent, and the opportunities for development have been puzzling.

Yes, the organization was forced to adjust its developmental timeline when Mark Williams suffered a shoulder injury in September that required surgery on his left shoulder. Suddenly, the buffer that would have allowed Khaman Maluach to develop behind Williams and Oso Ighodaro in the rotation was gone. The second-year big man out of Duke was now positioned to receive considerably more playing time than the organization likely anticipated entering the season.

While that certainly wasn't the original plan, there was a potential silver lining. Reluctance to play Maluach could no longer serve as an excuse for limiting his opportunities. The Suns were going to need him out of sheer necessity, and that necessity could provide the very developmental experience this organization had spent the summer emphasizing.

Those opportunities have certainly presented themselves early on this season. Through the first six games of the season, Khaman Maluach has started all six, averaging 7.2 points, 6.0 rebounds, 1.2 assists, 0.5 steals, and 1.0 blocks in 19.4 minutes per game.

The opportunity to develop has been there, but I've noticed a troubling trend recently that has me asking one simple question: What are we doing here? Because winning basketball games certainly isn't what we're doing right now, and of the many reasons why that's the case, the minutes being given to Khaman Maluach aren't anywhere near my top 10.

In fact, his absence becomes increasingly noticeable on a team that desperately lacks size and has been horrific at consistently securing rebounds. Phoenix ranks 29th in the NBA in rebounds per game at 39.5 and dead last in rebound percentage at 45.3%. Yet despite those struggles, the Suns continue to limit the playing time of one of the few players on the roster capable of providing a legitimate interior presence.

And that brings me to the trend that's becoming increasingly difficult to understand. In each of the last three games, Khaman Maluach hasn't played a single minute in the fourth quarter. Against both Denver and Golden State, he was pulled with 7:04 remaining in the third. Against Portland on Wednesday night, his final appearance ended with 6:09 left in the third. Why?

Last night against the Trail Blazers, Jordan Ott followed the same substitution pattern we've grown accustomed to seeing early this season. Maluach starts the game before exiting midway through the first quarter. He returns midway through the second, plays roughly five minutes, and then starts the second half. But somewhere around the midway point of the third quarter, Ott pulls him from the game, never to be seen again.

We've now witnessed that exact pattern in four of the Suns' first six games, and for a team supposedly committed to development, it's becoming increasingly difficult to understand why. So let's try to figure it out.

Khaman Maluach Substitution Patterns | https://nbarotations.info/player/1642863

Without Khaman Maluach, the Suns are left relying on either small-ball lineups or Oso Ighodaro at the five. And while neither option is inherently problematic, the results have been inconsistent, particularly on the boards.

Last night against Portland, Phoenix was actually holding its own on the glass. Yes, the Suns were trailing by 13 points when Maluach exited with 6:09 remaining in the third quarter, but they were winning the rebounding battle 27-25. Over the final 18:09, however, Portland outrebounded Phoenix by 10 and won the offensive rebounding battle 10-5. By the final buzzer, the Trail Blazers had secured a 47-39 advantage on the glass.

It's important to note that these numbers reflect the team's performance before and after Maluach's final substitution, rather than exclusively when he was on or off the court.

The data tells a slightly different story against Golden State. Through the first 28:56, Phoenix had been outrebounded 28-20. But over the final 19:04, after Maluach exited for the final time, the Suns actually outrebounded the Warriors 17-16. Against Denver, Phoenix held a 22-19 rebounding advantage before Maluach's final substitution, then was outrebounded 21-20 the rest of the way.

So what gives? Why is Maluach being banned from the chat after the two-and-a-half quarters of play? Across these three games, Phoenix was outrebounded 72-69 before Maluach's final departures and 59-49 afterward. That's a three-rebound deficit becoming a 10-rebound deficit, despite the latter periods being considerably shorter.

Welp, we're done here. It's clear Ott doesn't know what he's doing. But wait. As Rafiki once wisely said, "Look harder…"

Rather than evaluating the rebounding numbers based on the point at which Maluach permanently exits the game, let's examine how Phoenix actually performs on the glass when he's on the court compared with when he's sitting on the bench.

Against Portland, Maluach played 15:51, during which the Suns were outrebounded 16-12, with the Trail Blazers collecting three offensive rebounds. During the 32:09 he spent on the bench, Portland still held the advantage, though the margin was considerably smaller, 31-27. Phoenix secured 42.9% of the recorded rebounds with Maluach playing, compared with 46.6% when he was off the floor.

Against Golden State, the disparity was even more noticeable. Phoenix was down seven rebounds in the rebounding battle with Maluach on the court and even when he was on the bench. The Suns secured only 36.0% of available rebounds during his minutes, compared with 50.0% when he wasn't playing.

And against Denver? Phoenix was even on the glass with Maluach playing and +2 with him on the bench. The Suns collected 50.0% of recorded rebounds when he was on the court and 51.7% when he was off.

Looking at the three games in which Malauch was pulled early, cumulatively, you find that when Malauch was on the court for 46:23, the team was outbounded by 11. Off the court for 97:37? The team was -2.

There's one variable in all of this that we simply don't have an answer to. We don't know how Maluach would perform in these fourth quarters if he were actually given the opportunity. We can evaluate what happens during his minutes and compare those numbers with what occurs when he's on the bench.

The numbers certainly complicate the argument that Maluach's absence is directly responsible for Phoenix's rebounding struggles. In these three games, the Suns actually rebounded at a higher percentage when he wasn't on the floor, although the degree of that advantage varied considerably from game to game. That's an interesting finding, especially given the eye test against Portland, where the Suns appeared to struggle considerably after his final departure. The full on/off data paints a more nuanced picture.

Khaman Maluach: Season On/Off | https://hoopsjunkie.io/player/khaman-maluach

This is where the conversation becomes particularly interesting, because at what point do you prioritize development over rebounding percentages when a player is on or off the court? Maluach hasn't looked great to start the season, but he's certainly been serviceable. And for a team that desperately lacks size, he's somebody who should probably be seeing a little more playing time at this point.

But in the grand scheme of things, when you're looking at a three-game sample in which the rebounding differential is minus-nine, I don't believe that's enough to justify limiting the opportunities and potential growth of a young center who needs experience to develop. Especially when you consider that Maluach has consistently demonstrated a desire to compete and remain engaged. This isn't somebody whose struggles stem from a poor attitude or a lack of effort.

He's a young player learning how to navigate the NBA, and perhaps we're overanalyzing a handful of fleeting moments rather than allowing him to work through those experiences.

You have to eventually take the training wheels off and let the kid learn, right? Is it too soon? Apparently, the coaching staff believes so.

But at some point, the Suns have to decide what they're actually trying to accomplish this season. If winning is the priority, the results suggest their current approach isn't working. And if development is supposed to be the foundation for the future, Maluach needs opportunities to make mistakes, learn from them, and grow. Those objectives don't have to be mutually exclusive. But keeping the training wheels on while the team continues losing accomplishes very little. Especially when the kid is never given a chance to finish the ride.

#2766. George Russell opens up on mental exhaustion after frustrating 2026 F1 season

George Russell has admitted he is mentally exhausted after a season in which he has repeatedly had to overcome challenges.

The Mercedes driver started 2026 as the favourite for the title, but after a string of issues outside of his control and incredible performances from his team-mate Kimi Antonelli, he watched on as the Italian became world champion in Mexico.

Speaking to the media at Interlagos on Thursday, Russell said that even reaching Brazil, where he celebrated his first Formula 1 win in 2022, had not lifted him.

"As I said, I probably just feel a bit exhausted this season of constantly picking myself back up," he said. "When you get kicked to the ground, you pick yourself back up, then you get kicked down again, you pick yourself back up and I was hoping to do that maybe twice in the season not every other weekend, really.

"When you get to a point of this season, you're away from home for three weeks in a row and you have another race like what happened in Mexico where a chance of victory, a chance at the podium just disappears totally outside of your control, is tough to deal with. It's very tough to deal with.

"So Brazil was a place that I love. I've got great memories. Do I come in with high expectations? Honestly, no. But looking forward to next year, for sure."

The Briton revealed he had gone back through the whole season with his engineers after Mexico and found that only six races had been free of problems.

"14 of those races, we've had things that have been what we thought was bad luck," he said. "But we need to start questioning things more deeply when it's happening so often, and especially on our side."

Russell is currently fourth in the drivers' standings on 250 points, 11 points behind Red Bull's Max Verstappen, who sits second on 261 points, and nine points behind Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton, who sits third on 259 points.

#2763. LeBron James' lawyers send cease and desist to AI sports-betting app that used his name and likeness

Attorneys for Philadelphia 76ers star LeBron James sent a cease and desist letter to an AI sports-betting app that used a popular nickname for James and released an ad featuring his likeness, according to Front Office Sports.

Bron AI, a sports-gambling app, put out the ad Wednesday. In it, an AI version of James can be seen placing bets on NBA outcomes.

The ad, which has already been taken down on X, never showed James' face in AI, but showed a basketball player who looked a lot like James from behind. The player in the ad was wearing a No. 23 jersey that read "Bron" on the back, making it an exceptionally obvious reference to James.

In the cease and desist letter, which was obtained by Front Office Sports, James' attorneys make it clear James "neither approved any use and/or exploitation of, nor authorized or granted permission" to his name or likeness being used in the ad.

Additionally, James' attorneys pointed out that the 76ers star already has an "exclusive endorsement arrangement" with Polymarket and that the Bron AI ad appeared to show James' character placing bets on NBA games, which is "a very serious violation of NBA rules and regulations."

James is, apparently, not the only NBA star to issue a cease and desist letter to the company. James' former teammate, Los Angeles Lakers star Luka Dončić, reportedly also asked the company to stop using his likeness. Dončić's picture was used in the ad. Pictures of other athletes, such as Giannis Antetokounmpo, Jayden Daniels, Christian McCaffrey and Donovan Mitchell also appeared in the ad.

Given the egregious nature of the violation, Bron AI quickly pulled the ad from social media. It's unclear whether the company will face further backlash for the stunt.

#2753. Back surgery will keep Robert Kraft from Rob Gronkowski's Patriots Hall of Fame induction

Patriots owner Robert Kraft recently underwent back surgery, which will keep him sidelined on “injured reserve” and force him to miss Rob Gronkowski’s induction into the Patriots Hall of Fame on Saturday.

“As much pain as I was in before having surgery, it pains me even more to miss the ceremony,” Kraft, 85, told Mike Reiss of ESPN on Thursday.

Doctors ordered Kraft to stay off his feet, so he will also miss the Patriots’ game against the Packers on Sunday and the trip to Munich for a Week 10 game against the Lions.

Fans voted Gronkowski into the Patriots Hall of Fame in April in his first year of eligibility.

Gronkowski, having undergone multiple back surgeries during his playing career, understood Kraft’s absence, the owner said.

“I always told Gronk that in my next life, I wanted to come back as him, because I had never seen him have a bad day. But after a couple of back surgeries, I take that back. I never want to experience that again,” Kraft said.

#2750. European Roundup: Woltemade & Baur deliver strong performances after Klopp snub, Rose's Bournemouth record seventh straight win, Hürzeler's Brighton yet to concede

German coaches Marco Rose and Fabian Hürzeler succeeded once again with their English clubs, while Nick Woltemade and Mika Baur delivered strong performances after missing out from Germany's squad.

It wasn't all smooth sailing for Rose at the start of his Bournemouth reign, but the Cherries have extended their winning streak to seven games with a 3-1 win at Sparta Prague on Thursday evening. The visitors missed a first-half penalty-kick before securing a comeback win against their ten-man hosts.

USMNT international Tyler Adams scored in the European stage for the first time since his goal that helped RB Leipzig beat Atlético Madrid in the 2019/20 Champions League quarter-final round. Bournemouth are one of the three teams with a perfect Europa League record after four matchdays, alongside Benfica and Ferencváros, who stunned AC Milan with a 2-0 win at San Siro.

From 108 participating clubs, fellow Premier League side Brighton are the only team yet to concede a goal in UEFA competitions as they beat Getafe in Spain with Malick Yalcouye's solitary strike. Hürzeler's men sit in fifth place in the early standings, with Lugano, Panathinaikos, Twente and Monaco winning all their respective first three games in Conference League.

Germany U21 international Paris Brunner had his goal ruled out by VAR for an offside in Monaco's 2-0 win over FC Nordsjælland. The 20-year-old was a candidate for a first Germany call-up, but the name of the former BVB youngster wasn't found when Jürgen Klopp announced the squad earlier on Thursday.

Similarly, Baur and Woltemade helped their respective clubs to massive European wins after they failed to keep their spots in Germany's setup. Baur's Celtic recorded their first points in Europa League with an entertaining 3-2 win over Beşiktaş.

Woltemade once again started for Juventus as the Serie A outfit returned home with three points from AZ Alkmaar. The 24-year-old registered his fifth direct goal involvement of the competition, with an assist to former Eintracht Frankfurt striker Randal Kolo Muani in a 2-1 win for the visitors.

Marten Winkler is another German striker who has been performing well in Europe as he scored in back-to-back Europa League games for Anderlecht. Like the former Hertha BSC player, FC Midtjylland's Kjell Wätjen was a 2. Bundesliga midfielder last term with VfL Bochum.

However, the ex-Dortmund youth midfielder had a difficult night on Thursday as his first-half red card led to his club's 6-1 home defeat to Ajax. The historic Dutch side missed Julian Brandt due to an injury, but Germany's current first-choice goalkeeper Marc-André ter Stegen and Thilo Kehrer played the entire game.

#2748. Walker Kessler admitted Domantas Sabonis outplayed him before strong fourth quarter

Prior to Wednesday's fourth quarter, Walker Kessler was sitting on five points, three rebounds and two steals — far lesser production than he'd proven capable of thus far in this season. Then, he exploded for a 10-point, five-rebound, four-block, one-steal final frame to finish with 15 points, eight rebounds, four blocks and one steal. Those are numbers much more in line with the 25-year-old's early season signature.

Kessler's counterpart in the middle was Sacramento Kings center Domantas Sabonis. He's a rugged, brawny big man who's unafraid to launch elbows and hips into defenders for space down low and also threads passes to teammates for easy scores. Before that fourth-quarter renaissance, Kessler recognized the Lithuanian veteran — who logged 16 points, 17 rebounds (six on the offensive glass), one assist and one steal — was getting the best of him.

"He's a very, very talented player. Really physical player," Kessler told reporters after the Los Angeles Lakers' 116-103 win on Wednesday. "Definitely got my tail kicked a little bit in the first three quarters. But I relied on my teammates and they did a good job of encouraging me … At the end of the day, just trying to win and started to roll my way a little bit."

While likely past his All-NBA apex at this stage of his career, the 30-year-old Sabonis remains a good player and tough cover. For Kessler to struggle through three quarters but still stay in the fight mentally to bounce back and help fuel a third straight Lakers victory is encouraging. Of course, the white-hot exploits of Luka Dončić, who notched his fourth consecutive 40-point outing, didn't ding Los Angeles' win probability either.

Kessler will face another big, strong body Friday night when Donovan Clingan and the West-leading, 6-1 Portland Trail Blazers come to town. It'll mark both the Lakers' second meeting of the year with Portland and their second NBA Cup Group Play game. After blowing a big lead to the Golden State Warriors last Friday in their opening NBA Cup matchup of 2026-27, they must win this one to maintain any hope of advancing to the Quarterfinals. Tipoff is schedule for 7 p.m.
