#2627. NBA Power Rankings: Warriors fly into top 10 with rejuvenated Stephen Curry, 76ers pushing for top spot

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

After the Warriors' win over Phoenix on Monday, their fifth straight (something they never managed last season), Stephen Curry was asked what about this year's squad feels different from the one that finished with 37 wins a year ago.

"I mean, Yax," Curry laughed, stating the obvious when it comes to the historic start of Warriors' rookie Yaxel Lendeborg. "BP [Brandin Podziemski] taking another step forward. B-Will [Brandon Williams] has been great for us off the bench, giving us something we haven't had in a while. We've had some individual production that's been pretty cool, some standout guys who've made their presence felt night after night.

"But I think collectively," Curry continued, "we're probably a little bit more prepared on the details of what we're trying to do, and not just taking for granted that you can just play like the Warriors of old and expect good things to happen."

Curry didn't elaborate on these "details" on which the Warriors are more focused this season, but it looks about the same on the statistical surface. They're playing at the same pace. Making the same amount of 3s. They're still a high-turnover offense. They remain small, collectively old and not particularly athletic. They own a nearly identical 114-ish defensive rating, which at the moment has them ranked as a bottom-10 unit. Their spot-up, pick-and-roll, transition and isolation frequencies are all pretty much the same, per Synergy.

Which is to say, the Warriors are, in fact, playing like the Warriors. They look so good, that they've jumped 15 spots this week into the top 10 of our weekly NBA Power Rankings. Let's break down three reasons why.

Anyone who says they can see slippage in Curry's game must be looking through one hell of a high-powered microscope. He's scoring more than a point a minute (30 PPG in 28.8 MPG). The only other player doing that, with at least 100 minutes played, is Luka Dončić.

Get this: According to Cleaning the Glass, the 137.4 points that Curry is currently scoring per 100 shot attempts registers as a career high. He's taking more than 10 3-pointers a night and connecting at a 43% clip. On Monday, he finally missed a free throw after making 51 straight to start the year.

So yeah, Curry is still Curry. The difference is, he's got a real co-star again (remember, this team was tracking toward a conference finals trip when Jimmy Butler first came over) in the form a 24-year-old rookie.

Even knowing Curry's greatness, just about everyone pegged Golden State as a lottery team this year. They may still end up there, but at the moment Lendeborg has completely revived a team that we had all left for dead. He's the only rookie in history other than Larry Bird to post at least 100 points, 40 rebounds and 20 assists through his first five games. He's just the third player in Warriors history to average north of 20 PPG (22.3) over his first seven games of his career, joining Wilt Chamberlain and Rick Barry. In the win over the Clippers on Sunday, he became the fourth rookie in history log a game with at least 37 points and five assists on 85% true shooting.

Lendeborg is tracking toward Rookie of the Year and honest All-Star consideration. He has given the Warriors a legit first option without Curry on the court, and, in tandem, he massively eases Curry's burden as a creator. The guy is already a pick-and-roll machine and, at the moment, the most efficient isolation scorer in the league.

For some reason Podziemski has become a punching bag for a lot of Warriors fans, but he's been a winning player from day one (just go look at his on/off splits dating back to his rookie year). With Butler out, and until Lendeborg came along, Podziemski was the only Warrior other than Curry who could generate real paint pressure.

This season, Podziemski is putting it all together to the tune of a career-high 17 points, five assists and five boards per game. Once again, the splits tell the tale: The Warriors have outscored opponents by 50 points with Podziemski on the floor so far this year, by far the team high.

Suddenly the Warriors have three to four guys on any given night who can break a defense down, and with that you're seeing these support-staff guys like Georges Niang, Gui Santos, De'Anthony Melton, Gary Payton II, Will Richard, Al Horford, and even Charles Bassey (who has gone from taking DNPs to putting up 25 points and 18 boards over the last two games) to ride shotgun on a top-five offense.

#2626. Week 9 Super Bowl stock report: Jeffery Simmons trade legitimizes Bears, QB injuries tank Ravens

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The NFL trade deadline is less than a week away, so a flurry of impactful moves could be on the way as Super Bowl contenders gear up for the stretch run. Even if the biggest transactions are already complete, this year's deadline will go down as a significant one, because the Chicago Bears proved in Week 8 how the acquisition of one star can flip a season. Jeffery Simmons elevated their defense in his first game following last week's blockbuster trade and rounded the Bears into an even more legitimate championship hopeful.

The Baltimore Ravens just made a move themselves at quarterback, but it doesn't come close to lifting the team the way Simmons does. Their top two options sustained injuries last week that could hold both of them out for the year, so in order to remain competitive in the AFC North, Baltimore brought in Arizona's Jacoby Brissett. There are several other teams to monitor as well ahead of the Nov. 10 deadline.

Week 9 is light on showdowns between top-tier contenders, but there are still a few contests — like the "Monday Night Football" battle featuring the Buffalo Bills and Minnesota Vikings — that will potentially reshape the title race.

Here are the latest trends in the Super Bowl hunt heading into Week 9.

A single move ahead of the NFL trade deadline elevated the Bears out of the pack of ordinary Super Bowl contenders and into the top tier of championship hopefuls. They suddenly own the third-shortest odds to roll through the postseason.

While the San Francisco 49ers are still the team to beat in the NFC until proven otherwise, the Bears' momentum is even more palpable, and it is beginning to feel like the conference runs through Chicago. Monday's 34-17 win on the road over the Seattle Seahawks might have been a passing of the torch from last year's champions to the best team of 2026.

Simmons unlocked all kinds of possibilities when he arrived by way of the Tennessee Titans. The three-time All-Pro defensive tackle recorded his first tackle as a Bear on the game's first play from scrimmage and earned his first sack on the following series. He dominated from start to finish and added another tackle for loss and a pass breakup in the fourth quarter. This is a new kind of weapon on the defensive front and one that gives coordinator Dennis Allen the freedom to blitz less frequently and still get pressure on the quarterback. That is an invaluable opportunity for a team that previously relied on the blitz at one of the NFL's highest rates.

The only weakness on this Bears team now resides in the secondary, and Simmons' arrival should mask it to a noticeable extent. Everything else about the Bears is championship-caliber. Ben Johnson's offense might finish the year as the highest-scoring operation in the league, Caleb Williams is on an MVP trajectory, Luther Burden III is breaking out in real time and the run game remains prolific with D'Andre Swift leading the charge. Now, the defense should be capable of at least holding up its end of the deal, if not outright leading the charge in some games.

The NFC North is anyone's division. Chicago now boasts the second-best offense and second-best defense, and as a newly minted well-rounded team, that might be enough to take command and secure a top-four seed in the postseason. And with the best defensive lineman in the world and a burgeoning superstar at quarterback, the No. 1 seed is now in play, too.

Year after year, the Ravens feel the wrath of injuries at the most important position. Lamar Jackson has only played two full seasons since 2021, and the contrast in record with and without him is appalling. Now that he is slated to miss extended time with his second injury of the year — a thumb issue that requires surgery — this season is trending in the same direction as 2021, 2022 and 2025 when his absences prevented Baltimore from vying for a championship.

What's more, backup Tyler Huntley is done for the season with turf toe, which leaves undrafted rookie Joe Fagnano as the starter for Week 9. The trade set to bring Jacoby Brissett to town does raise the floor quite a bit, but there is no getting back to the ceiling Jackson provides.

Fagnano was the emergency third quarterback in Week 8 and was thrust into the first action of his young career when both signal-callers ahead of him departed with injuries in the first half of the loss to the Bills, and the UConn product is now tasked with keeping the offense afloat on "Thursday Night Football." The Ravens also signed Kedon Slovis off the Packers' practice squad and added Austin Reed to their own practice squad, making him the likely third quarterback against the Jaguars on "Thursday Night Football."

Once Brissett arrives, it will be his show. But he was just benched in Arizona last week, so the Ravens cannot bank on him delivering enough of an upgrade over the other bleak options to keep the season alive.

Less than one half of football entirely changed the outlook for Baltimore's season. The injuries in the opening minutes of the matchup against Buffalo relegated the Ravens from Super Bowl contention to a potential last-place finish in their own division. Their odds to win it all plummeted to +10000.

Unless Jackson can recover quickly from his surgery and limit his injured reserve stint to four games or only slightly more, this will likely be a lost season. And with the potential for him to miss the rest of the year, Brissett possibly overseeing a decent offense is the only real source of optimism in Baltimore.

The balance of power shifted immensely in the AFC North over the last week. The Ravens' quarterback injuries cleared the path forward for the other three teams, and the Steelers' head-to-head win over the Browns prompted a shakeup at the top with Pittsburgh securing sole possession of first place. After their Week 9 bye, the Steelers will have an opportunity to build separation in a second showdown with the Bengals. They beat Cincinnati in their first matchup.

The reunion between Aaron Rodgers and Mike McCarthy injected new life into the offense ahead of the season, and the results are playing out on game days. The passing attack is effective even without a full-strength wide receiver room, and Jaylen Warren leads an invigorated run game that ranks third in the league in EPA per rush. And on the other side of the ball, first-year defensive coordinator Patrick Graham is easily among the best new assistant coaches in football. His unit ranks in the top eight in scoring defense (No. 3), total defense (No. 6), run defense (No. 3), third-down defense (No. 8), red-zone defense (No. 2) and takeaways (No. 3).

Sunday's win over Cleveland was the greatest example yet of how everything has come together in 2026. The 27-6 triumph gave the Steelers their largest margin of victory of the season, while the six points they allowed were their fewest of the year.

Sunday, 1 p.m., CBS, stream on Paramount+

This is a get-up-off-the-mat game for the Panthers, who lost their last two contests by a combined 38 points but were fortunate to find a one-score margin in their last outing. Bryce Young's early-season success is a thing of the past, as it seems opponents have cracked the code on stopping his breakout. The Broncos pose another stiff challenge. Denver, meanwhile, is the significantly stronger Super Bowl contender of the two and rides a four-game win streak into this cross-country trip. Sean Payton's squad is 15-0 in one-score games dating back to the middle of last season and is 5-0 in games decided by seven points or fewer this year alone. How sustainable is that? Apparently quite sustainable.

The quarterback showdown between Drake Maye and Jordan Love is the best Week 9 has to offer. Between them, there are just over 4,200 yards and 31 touchdowns on the season, and they carry identical records into their showdown. Every time the Patriots have won a game, the Packers have too. Both teams suffered their three losses in the same weeks, too. That means both are playing their best football right now with four wins in the last five weeks.

Minnesota's league-leading defense will be put to the test for the second consecutive week. Last time out, it faced the NFL's top offense and held it to 19 points. This time, it meets the second-best unit with Josh Allen coming to town. If the Vikings could limit the Lions to just two touchdowns, then they should feel confident about their ability to contain Allen and his group. The bigger question is whether Kevin O'Connell's offense can do enough to take advantage. The unit has been lifeless even in its most favorable matchups, so a banged-up Kyler Murray (hamstring) may not be entirely trustworthy against the Bills and their less-than-perfect defense.

#2624. MLB offseason bold predictions: Tarik Skubal breaks records, World Series champ gets a deal, a FA frenzy, more

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

With the Brewers crowned World Series champions, the 2026-27 offseason is underway. We're still waiting for the first significant free agent signing or trade, which isn't unusual less than a week into the offseason. Give it another week or so and the action will pick up. Before the hot stove really gets burning, here are 10 bold predictions for the 2026-27 offseason. Remember, all geniuses were called crazy at first.

Yoshinobu Yamamoto's $325 million deal with the Dodgers is the largest pitching contract in history, and our first bold prediction says Tarik Skubal, this offseason's undisputed No. 1 free agent, will beat that. Specifically, he'll sign a contract that is closer to $400 million in value than $300 million, which is another way of saying he'll clear $350 million and break Yamamoto's record for total dollars by a good bit. Scott Boras, Skubal's agent, likes to break contract records with room to spare, not just by a tiny bit. Skubal is the best free agent starter since Yamamoto, and the best free agent starter with MLB experience since Gerrit Cole in 2019. It's a very thin free agent class with few places to (wisely) spend money. The bet here is a team steps up and gives Skubal a record deal.

Milwaukee's thing over the last few years has been trading its top players a year before free agency (Corbin Burnes, Freddy Peralta, Devin Williams, etc.) and obviously it has worked for them. William Contreras is at that point now: he's scheduled to hit the open market next offseason. This next bold prediction says the Brewers will buck that trend and instead sign the World Series MVP to a long-term extension that keeps him in Milwaukee for at least another few years, if not the rest of his career. How does six years at $24 million a pop sound? That would be $144 million total and the richest contract given to a catcher in the last 13 years, clearing Will Smith's $140 extension with the Dodgers. The World Series champs keep their most irreplaceable player. It has been foretold.

Every offseason is important, and this one is extra important for new Astros GM Randy Flores, who must figure out what to do with third baseman Isaac Paredes and shortstop Jeremy Peña, both a year away from free agency. Keeping Peña and trading Paredes, and installing Carlos Correa at the hot corner, is the sensible move. This bold prediction says the opposite will happen. The Astros will trade Peña and keep Paredes, and figure out their 2027 infield alignment later. Houston needs help up and down the roster, particularly on the mound, and I think the offers for Peña will simply be too great for Flores to ignore. It will be similar to the Kyle Tucker trade two years ago. The Astros don't have to move Peña, but the offers will get to a point where they just can't say no.

On one hand, keeping the offense intact and adding some pitching would be a viable offseason plan for the Braves. On the other hand, can they really run it back with the same offense that flatlined after June 1 and in the NLDS? It might be time to shake things up a bit, and I boldly predict it will happen. Ronald Acuña Jr., Drake Baldwin, Michael Harris II, and Matt Olson aren't going anywhere. No team will take the current version of Austin Riley and the six years (!) remaining on his contract. That leaves Ozzie Albies and I suppose Sean Murphy, though the latter is well into role player status now. Does that make this bold prediction a "the Braves will trade Albies" prediction? Yeah, I guess it does. It feels like things are getting a little stale in Atlanta and it's time to change up a core.

You could argue Freddy Peralta is the second-best free agent starter behind Skubal. You could also argue it's Trevor Rogers, who doesn't have Peralta's pedigree or track record, but has strong under-the-hood performance indicators, the kind that project well into the future and get players paid. So, for this bold prediction, I'll say that Rogers signs a richer deal than Peralta, even though the latter is the more famous player and has been better in their careers to date. It'll be close. I can see Rogers getting something in the $125 million range and Peralta signing for right around $120 million, but, in the end, Rogers will sign for more guaranteed dollars because he's a year and a half younger and teams love nothing more than players they believe have untapped upside. That's Rogers, not Peralta.

After the Dodgers swept in the NLCS, there were calls to infuse some youth into the roster, and, honestly, they need it. Fortunately, Los Angeles has one of the best prospects in the game in the precocious Josue De Paula, who was so impressive late in the season. Trading an outfielder to clear a spot for De Paula seems like such an obvious move that I'm not sure this prediction qualifies as bold. Andy Pages and Kyle Tucker aren't going anywhere, which leaves Teoscar Hernández. How about a trade that sends Hernández back to the Blue Jays? It's a one-year commitment, the Blue Jays badly need over-the-fence power, and the fan base already loves the guy. Teoscar to Toronto as what amounts to their George Springer replacement. I boldly predict it.

Every offseason, there are two teams that appear to match up so well that a trade feels inevitable. Last offseason, it was the Brewers and Mets for a Freddy Peralta deal. This offseason, it's the Cubs and Yankees. The Cubs need rotation help and have some young position players to spare (like Matt Shaw). The Yankees need infield help and have starting pitching to trade (like Will Warren). I'm not saying Shaw for Warren will happen or even should happen. I'm just saying Chicago's and New York's trade chips and roster needs align very well, and when that happens, a trade typically comes together. This bold prediction says the Cubs will send a position player to the Yankees for a starting pitcher, with maybe some other pieces involved on both sides.

There are trade rumors involving a Mariners starting pitcher every offseason and there's a good reason for that. They have a lot of really good starters and teams want them. The Mariners currently have Kade Anderson, Logan Gilbert, Emerson Hancock, George Kirby, Bryce Miller, and Bryan Woo lined up for their 2027 rotation. They could keep them all because pitching depth has a way of disappearing, sure, but Seattle needed another bat even before Randy Arozarena became a free agent. This next bold prediction says the Mariners finally trade one of their starters in an arm-for-bat deal. I'll say Kirby, who is two years away from free agency, is the one to go. Gilbert is a one-year rental but the better pitcher. The others all have longer control than Kirby.

After coming out of the gate so well in April and May, Munetaka Murakami finished right where the pundits expected. He hit .207 and had the highest strikeout rate among qualified hitters, but he also slugged 35 home runs in only 127 games. Hanshin Tigers third baseman Teruaki Sato, who will be posted for MLB teams this offseason, is similar to Murakami as a strikeout-prone lefty with huge power. This bold prediction says Sato will double Murakami's contract with the White Sox (two years and $34 million) because he's a better bet to stay at third base, a position that is barren in free agency, and because Murakami provided proof of concept. He showed that a player with big contact concerns in Japan can indeed succeed stateside, even if it is an eyesore at times. Four years and $68 million for Sato, perhaps with an opt out that makes the $68 million not really $68 million.

Dec. 1 is of course when the collective bargaining agreement expires and the owners are expected to lock out the players. My final bold prediction says free agents and teams will get out ahead of the potential lockout and sign in November. Players won't want to wait until who knows when to sign and teams will want to lock in contracts so they can be grandfathered into whatever the next CBA brings. MLB free agency tends to be slow-moving. Last offseason, only one of our top 10 free agents signed in November, and that was Shota Imanaga taking the qualifying offer. Only three other top 10 free agents signed in December. The other six signed on Jan. 14 or later. This offseason will be the opposite, I boldly predict. There will be a flurry of activity in November and at least seven of our top 10 free agents will put pen to paper before a potential lockout.

#2622. Why Ravens should trade Derrick Henry: Don't let Baltimore's QB woes drag down 'King Henry'

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

As the NFL's Nov. 10 trade deadline approaches, several notable players are on the trade bubble. One notable player who should also be in discussion is Baltimore Ravens running back Derrick Henry.

Henry, 32, is a future Hall of Famer in the middle of his 11th season in the NFL and third season with the Ravens. Through eight games, Henry has rushed for 632 yards and eight touchdowns and has carried the ball a league-high 158 times. His 4.0 yards per carry this season is nearly a full yard lower than his career average.

Henry started the season with a bang. He had 144 yards and three touchdowns in Baltimore's season-opener and scored eight touchdowns in the season's first five games. His production has tapered off since, though. Henry (who has just one other 100-yard rushing performance this season) has averaged just 52 rushing yards over Baltimore's past three games and has scored just one touchdown over the past month.

Below are the three reasons why Baltimore should consider trading Henry sometime over the next week.

While they are an even 4-4 through eight games, the Ravens' season is, for all intents and purposes, over, unless Jacoby Brissett can save Baltimore's sinking ship.

After a 4-1 start, the Ravens have lost three straight games to fall to last place in the AFC North division. Lamar Jackson (right thumb injury) might miss the rest of the season, and backup Tyler Huntley (turf toe) will be out for the remainder of the campaign. Those injuries have compelled the Ravens to trade for Brissett, who was recently demoted to third string in Arizona.

Baltimore's decision to trade for Brissett is a clear indication that the Ravens don't intend to throw the white flag. While that is admirable, Baltimore would be better served making decisions now that can improve their team in the long term.

Unless Brissett plays at a Pro Bowl level, the Ravens aren't going anywhere this season. They were a solid team with Jackson, an average team with Huntley and are now a substandard team with Brissett. That's the same Brissett who was benched this past Sunday after going 10-of-23 (with an interception) against a Cowboys defense that has been one of the league's worst this season.

Baltimore has been outscored a combined 71-23 over its last two games. The offensive line is substandard, and the defense has struggled to stop anyone in the red zone. The issues in Baltimore go well beyond the quarterback.

Looking at their remaining schedule, the Ravens' Week 10 home game against the winless Chargers is the only game where Baltimore would be a betting favorite. There's a chance that Brissett can help the Ravens claw to eight or nine wins, but unless Jackson is able to make a late-season return, the odds of Baltimore making the playoffs — and doing anything if they get there — are slim to none.

Baltimore would undoubtedly get a decent return for Henry, whose name alone is worth a second-round pick. Several playoff-contending teams would surely be interested in acquiring a running back of Henry's caliber for the stretch run.

The Giants and Vikings are among the teams most likely to be interested in acquiring Henry. The Bengals might be, too, but it's unlikely that Baltimore would trade Henry to a division rival.

New York is especially interesting. Would the Ravens facilitate a trade that would reunite Henry with their former coach, John Harbaugh? One would think that they would if the Giants made them the right offer.

As noted above, Henry's name alone is worth a second-round pick. At this point, it's a pretty open market for running backs who might be available. The Colts' Jonathan Taylor tops that list, with Tennessee's Tony Pollard coming in behind him.

Taylor would be the top running back available regardless of Henry's status. Taylor is significantly younger and has been more productive in recent weeks (although he was barely used during the Colts' recent loss to the Jaguars). But because there are multiple teams that could use help at running back, whoever loses out on getting Taylor (assuming the Colts trade him) would surely try to get Henry if he is available.

As far as a trade is concerned, it only takes one team to drive up the price. If a bidding war is created, it's possible the Ravens could even get more than a second-round pick for Henry. And while a first-round pick might be a stretch, anything is possible, which is why the Ravens should at least explore the possibility of moving Henry, whose trade value will probably never be higher than it is now.

Baltimore GM Eric DeCosta should be commended for pairing Jackson and Henry together back in 2024. Two of the most dynamic players at their position, Jackson and Henry powered the Ravens to a division title that season and came up a play short of playing for a trip to the Super Bowl.

Things have changed since then, though. Baltimore missed the playoffs last year and will probably miss the postseason again this season. Respectively, Henry and Jackson will be 33 and 30 before the start of next season. Their championship window as teammates is closing, if it hasn't closed already.

DeCosta should realize that he is beginning the process of turning over parts of his roster, including running back. Henry has been a great player for Baltimore, and DeCosta should reward him by giving him a chance to play for a contender.

As noted above, Henry is a surefire future Hall of Famer. He's third all-time in career touchdown runs and is closing in on being seventh all-time in career rushing yards. Henry's career also includes being just one of nine players with a 2,000-yard rushing season. His 1,921 yards in 2024 (his first year in Baltimore) is the most in NFL history for a player over 30.

Henry has done it all in his NFL career except get to and win a Super Bowl. Baltimore should give King Henry a chance to win his elusive crown before it's too late.
